content: The data provided outlines key findings on adolescent mortality, morbidity, and associated risk factors globally and across various regions, as reported by the World Health Organization (WHO) and other sources. 1. Adolescent Mortality Trends: The leading causes of death among adolescents vary by region, age, and sex. Globally, road injuries, self-harm, and drowning are significant contributors to adolescent mortality across most regions. In specific regions, other conditions dominate. For example: In African lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), meningitis and HIV/AIDS are major causes of death. In South-East Asian LMICs, diarrheal diseases and tuberculosis (TB) are prominent. Interpersonal violence is a leading cause of death in high-income countries (HICs) and LMICs in the Americas. Congenital anomalies are significant in European LMICs, HICs, and Western Pacific LMICs. Leukemia is a notable cause of death in Western Pacific LMICs. 2. Adolescent Mortality by Age and Sex: Among 10–14-year-olds globally, road injuries and diarrheal diseases are the leading causes of death for both males and females, followed by drowning and lower respiratory infections. For 15–19-year-olds, road injuries remain the leading cause of death for males, while maternal conditions and self-harm are significant for females. Tuberculosis and interpersonal violence also contribute to mortality in this age group. 3. Regional Variations in Mortality: In African LMICs, road injuries, diarrheal diseases, HIV/AIDS, and malaria are the leading causes of death among adolescents. In the Americas, interpersonal violence and road injuries are prominent, with leukemia and congenital anomalies also contributing. In the Eastern Mediterranean, diarrheal diseases, road injuries, and congenital anomalies are significant. In European LMICs, road injuries, drowning, and congenital anomalies are leading causes. In South-East Asia, diarrheal diseases, road injuries, and tuberculosis are major contributors. In Western Pacific LMICs, drowning, road injuries, and leukemia are significant causes of death. 4. Adolescent Morbidity Trends: Morbidity rates among adolescents, measured as Years Lived with Disability (YLDs), have shown little change globally from 2000 to 2019. However, African LMICs experienced the greatest decline, while HICs saw an upward trend. Older female adolescents (15–19 years) consistently exhibit higher morbidity rates compared to other groups, with a YLD rate of 6,911 per 100,000 in 2019. In contrast, the lowest morbidity rates are observed among 10–14-year-old males. 5. Leading Causes of Adolescent Morbidity: At the global level, non-communicable diseases (NCDs) dominate the top five causes of morbidity in both age groups (10–14 and 15–19 years). Iron deficiency anemia is the only communicable, maternal, perinatal, or nutritional condition consistently appearing in the top five. Mental health disorders, including depressive disorders, anxiety disorders, childhood behavioral disorders, and idiopathic intellectual disability, are the most common NCDs across all regions and age groups. 6. Regional Variations in Morbidity: In African LMICs, iron deficiency anemia, childhood behavioral disorders, and malaria are leading causes of morbidity. In the Americas, childhood behavioral disorders, migraines, and anxiety disorders are prominent. In the Eastern Mediterranean, iron deficiency anemia, anxiety disorders, and migraines are significant contributors. In European LMICs, childhood behavioral disorders, anxiety disorders, and migraines are leading causes. In South-East Asia, iron deficiency anemia, childhood behavioral disorders, and idiopathic intellectual disability are prominent. In Western Pacific LMICs, childhood behavioral disorders, anxiety disorders, and skin diseases are significant. 7. Risk Factors for Adolescent Health: The 2019 Global Burden of Disease study identified the top 10 risk factors for adolescent Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs), which combine mortality and morbidity. These include: Iron deficiency Unsafe water sources Unsafe sanitation Lack of access to handwashing facilities Low birth weight and short gestation Bullying victimization Particulate matter pollution Child growth failure Lead exposure Occupational ergonomic factors (notable among older adolescents) 8. Protective Factors for Adolescent Health: While the data primarily focuses on risk factors, protective factors are equally important in promoting adolescent health and well-being. These include access to education, supportive family environments, and community-based interventions to address mental health and prevent injuries. This detailed breakdown provides a comprehensive understanding of the global and regional trends in adolescent health, highlighting the importance of targeted interventions to address both mortality and morbidity in this vulnerable population.
